NONPROFIT CORPORATION DIRECTOR'S DUTY OF CARE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the statutory standard of care that governs how a director of a California nonprofit corporation performs the duties of a director, the statutory right of a director to rely on certain other sources in performing those duties, the resulting statutory liability protection, a separate and narrower statutory immunity available to uncompensated volunteer directors and officers, and who may bring an action to enforce these duties. California's Nonprofit Corporation Law states this standard three times, once for each of the three types of nonprofit corporation it recognizes — public benefit corporations (Corporations Code section 5231), mutual benefit corporations (section 7231), and religious corporations (section 9241) — and the wording differs among them in ways this Information Sheet identifies. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee's service as a director of Acme, Inc., organized as a stock corporation. This project's existing Director's Duty of Care and Business Judgment Rule Information Sheet covers Corporations Code section 309, which applies to general stock corporations, not nonprofit corporations; this document covers the separate nonprofit statutes instead. This project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet separately covers the regulated self-dealing-transaction and common-directorship safe-harbor rules for corporations under sections 310, 5233, and 7233; this document states the general duty-of-care standard those self-dealing statutes are carved out from, but does not restate the self-dealing rules themselves. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what these statutes provide; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether any specific decision, vote, or other conduct by Jordan Lee as a director of Acme, Inc. satisfied the standard described here, or whether any statutory liability protection or immunity described here would apply to any specific act or omission. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer.

THE DUTY-OF-CARE STANDARD FOR PUBLIC BENEFIT AND MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION DIRECTORS
California states an almost word-for-word identical duty-of-care standard for directors of public benefit corporations and directors of mutual benefit corporations. In both cases, a director must perform the duties of a director, including as a member of a board committee, (1) in good faith, (2) in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation, and (3) with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances. This is the standard against which Jordan Lee's performance of duties as a director of Acme, Inc. is measured, if Acme, Inc. is organized as a public benefit or mutual benefit corporation under California law; this clause states the standard itself and does not evaluate whether any specific decision by Jordan Lee met it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner that director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, director's standard of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5231.)
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(a), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, director's standard of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7231.)
  Known gap: These are two separate statutes in two separate Parts of the Nonprofit Corporation Law (Part 2, public benefit corporations, and Part 3, mutual benefit corporations), not two subdivisions of one section, so they are independent enactments — but their near-identical wording (differing only in “that director believes” versus “such director believes”) reflects a common origin in the same 1978 nonprofit corporation law revision, not independent corroboration of a general common-law rule. This clause covers only subdivision (a) of each section; the reliance right, liability protection, and self-dealing carve-out in the remaining subdivisions are addressed in the following two clauses, which show that the two statutes are not actually identical once those subdivisions are reached. This clause does not address religious corporations, which use a differently worded standard covered in a later clause of this document.

PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION DIRECTORS: RELIANCE RIGHTS, LIABILITY PROTECTION, AND THE SELF-DEALING CARVE-OUT
In performing the duties described in the preceding clause, a public benefit corporation director is entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports, or statements — including financial statements and other financial data — prepared or presented by corporate officers or employees the director believes reliable and competent, by counsel, independent accountants, or other experts as to matters within their professional competence, or by a board committee the director does not serve on and believes merits confidence, so long as the director acts in good faith and without knowledge that would make the reliance unwarranted. A director who performs duties consistently with this standard and reliance right has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, including for actions or omissions that exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which the corporation or its assets are dedicated — except as the self-dealing-transaction statute, Corporations Code section 5233, separately provides. This clause states what Jordan Lee is entitled to rely on and the resulting liability protection as a director of Acme, Inc., if organized as a public benefit corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by Jordan Lee in fact falls within these categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within that person’s professional or expert competence; or (3) A committee upon which the director does not serve that is composed exclusively of any or any combination of directors, persons described in paragraph (1), or persons described in paragraph (2), as to matters within the committee’s designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause that reliance to be unwarranted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(b), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5231.)
  "Except as provided in Section 5233, a person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which a corporation, or assets held by it, are dedicated."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(c), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, liability protection subject to the self-dealing carve-out (same section as the two citations above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5231.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of the same statute quoted in the preceding clause (Corporations Code section 5231) — they are not independent sources corroborating one another, only different subdivisions of one section. This document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 5233 (the self-dealing-transaction statute referenced by the “Except as provided in” language in subdivision (c)); this project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet addresses that statute's substance, and readers should consult it or Section 5233 directly rather than relying on this clause for that carve-out's content. This clause does not address the separate volunteer-director immunity statute (Section 5239), covered later in this document.

MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION DIRECTORS: RELIANCE RIGHTS AND LIABILITY PROTECTION
A mutual benefit corporation director is entitled to rely on the same three categories of sources as a public benefit corporation director — corporate officers or employees the director believes reliable and competent, counsel or other experts as to matters within their professional competence, and a board committee the director does not serve on and believes merits confidence — subject to the same good-faith and no-unwarranted-reliance conditions. A director who performs duties consistently with this standard and reliance right has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, including for actions or omissions that exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which the corporation's assets are dedicated. This clause states what Jordan Lee is entitled to rely on and the resulting liability protection as a director of Acme, Inc., if organized as a mutual benefit corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by Jordan Lee in fact falls within these categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within such person’s professional or expert competence; or (3) A committee upon which the director does not serve that is composed exclusively of any or any combination of directors, persons described in paragraph (1), or persons described in paragraph (2), as to matters within the committee’s designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(b), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7231.)
  "A person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which assets held by a corporation are dedicated."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(c), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, liability protection (same section as the citation above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7231.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of the same statute quoted two clauses above (Corporations Code section 7231) — not independent sources of one another. Unlike the parallel public benefit corporation statute's liability-protection subdivision quoted in the preceding clause, subdivision (c) of this mutual benefit corporation statute contains no “Except as provided in Section 7233” (the mutual benefit self-dealing statute) or similar cross-reference in its own text; the self-dealing carve-out for mutual benefit corporations instead appears in the separate volunteer-immunity statute, Section 7231.5, quoted later in this document, and only as to the volunteer directors and narrow category of corporations that statute covers. This clause reports that textual difference; it does not draw any conclusion about whether a compensated (non-volunteer) mutual benefit corporation director's liability protection under this section is, in substance, broader or narrower than a public benefit corporation director's when a self-dealing transaction is at issue — that would require analyzing Section 7233 and any case law construing it, neither of which this document verifies; no case law is cited anywhere in this document because a CourtListener search attempted during this research returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be retrieved.

RELIGIOUS CORPORATION DIRECTORS: A DIFFERENTLY WORDED STANDARD, WITH AN ADDED RELIANCE CATEGORY
A religious corporation director's duty-of-care standard shares the same good-faith and best-interests elements as the public benefit and mutual benefit corporation standards, but its care element is worded differently: instead of the care an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances, the statute requires the care that is appropriate under the circumstances, without using the phrase “ordinarily prudent person.” A religious corporation director may also rely on a fourth category of source unavailable to public benefit or mutual benefit corporation directors: religious authorities and ministers, priests, rabbis, or other persons whose position or duties in the religious organization the director believes justify reliance and confidence, on the same terms of belief in their reliability and competence as apply to the other reliance categories. This clause states what Jordan Lee is entitled to rely on as a director of Acme, Inc., if organized as a religious corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by Jordan Lee in fact falls within these categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as is appropriate under the circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(a), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, director's standard of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9241.)
  "Religious authorities and ministers, priests, rabbis, or other persons whose position or duties in the religious organization the director believes justify reliance and confidence and whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances, and without knowledge that would cause that reliance to be unwarranted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(b)(4), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, added reliance category for religious authorities (same section as the citation above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9241.)
  Known gap: This document does not determine, and no case law verified in this research addresses, whether the religious corporation standard's “appropriate under the circumstances” phrasing is functionally equivalent to, stricter than, or more lenient than the “ordinarily prudent person” phrasing used for public benefit and mutual benefit corporations; a CourtListener search on this topic returned a daily rate-limit error before any results were retrieved, so this document proceeds on the verified statutory text alone. This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b) of one statute (Corporations Code section 9241); the compensation/loan-resolution rule and the liability protection in the remaining subdivisions of the same section are addressed in the following clause.

RELIGIOUS CORPORATION DIRECTORS: COMPENSATION AND LOAN RESOLUTIONS, AND THE SECTION 9243 LIABILITY CARVE-OUT
California law specifically directs that the religious corporation director statute described in the preceding clause — not the religious corporation self-dealing statute, section 9243 — governs a director's action or omission regarding director or officer compensation, or a loan of money or property to, or a guaranty of the obligation of, any director or officer; a resulting board resolution is not voidable merely because directors who benefited from it participated in adopting it. Separately, a director who performs duties consistent with the standard and reliance right described in the preceding clause has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, except as section 9243 separately provides. This clause states what the statute provides on these two points as applied to Jordan Lee's service as a director of Acme, Inc., if organized as a religious corporation; it does not evaluate any specific compensation, loan, or guaranty resolution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The provisions of this section, and not Section 9243, shall govern any action or omission of a director in regard to the compensation of directors, as directors or officers, or any loan of money or property to or guaranty of the obligation of any director or officer. No obligation, otherwise valid, shall be voidable merely because directors who benefited by a board resolution to pay such compensation or to make such loan or guaranty participated in making such board resolution."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(c), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, compensation and loan/guaranty resolutions governed by this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9241.)
  "Except as provided in Section 9243, a person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge his or her obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat any purpose to which the corporation, or assets held by it, may be dedicated."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(d), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, liability protection subject to the Section 9243 carve-out (same section as the citation above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9241.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same statute quoted in the preceding clause (Corporations Code section 9241) — not independent sources of one another. This document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 9243 (the religious corporation self-dealing statute referenced in both subdivisions); readers should consult that section directly, or this project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet, rather than relying on this clause for its substance.

LIMITED PERSONAL-LIABILITY IMMUNITY FOR VOLUNTEER DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS OF PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATIONS
A separate statute limits a volunteer director's or volunteer executive officer's personal liability to a third party for monetary damages caused by a negligent act or omission in performing duties as a director or officer of a public-benefit-corporation-type nonprofit, if four conditions are all met: the act or omission was within the scope of the person's duties; it was performed in good faith; it was not reckless, wanton, intentional, or grossly negligent; and the resulting damages are covered by a liability insurance policy, or, if not covered, the corporation's board and the person made all reasonable efforts in good faith to obtain available liability insurance. This immunity does not eliminate or limit liability under the self-dealing statute (section 5233) or the statute governing certain loans and guaranties to directors and officers (section 5237), or in any action brought by the Attorney General. This clause states the conditions and carve-outs of this immunity as it could apply to Jordan Lee's uncompensated service as a director of Acme, Inc., if Jordan Lee serves without compensation and Acme, Inc. is a public benefit corporation; it does not determine whether Jordan Lee in fact qualifies as a “volunteer” under the statute's definition, whether any act or omission meets these conditions, or whether Acme, Inc. carries the insurance, or made the good-faith insurance-seeking efforts, the statute describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "There shall be no personal liability to a third party for monetary damages on the part of a volunteer director or volunteer executive officer of a nonprofit corporation subject to this part, caused by the director’s or officer’s negligent act or omission in the performance of that person’s duties as a director or officer, if all of the following conditions are met: (1) The act or omission was within the scope of the director’s or executive officer’s duties. (2) The act or omission was performed in good faith. (3) The act or omission was not reckless, wanton, intentional, or grossly negligent. (4) Damages caused by the act or omission are covered pursuant to a liability insurance policy issued to the corporation, either in the form of a general liability policy or a director’s and officer’s liability policy, or personally to the director or executive officer."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5239(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, volunteer director/officer immunity conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5239.)
  "This section does not eliminate or limit the liability of a director or officer for any of the following: (1) As provided in Section 5233 or 5237. (2) In any action or proceeding brought by the Attorney General."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5239(e), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, carve-outs from the volunteer immunity (same section as the citation above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5239.)
  Known gap: This statute (Corporations Code section 5239) applies only to causes of action based on acts or omissions occurring on or after January 1, 1988, by its own terms; this clause does not verify the statute's further subdivision addressing a modified insurance-inquiry standard for smaller public benefit corporations with an annual budget under $25,000 that are tax-exempt under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c)(3), which this document does not quote. This clause also does not address the differently scoped, narrower volunteer immunity statute that applies to certain mutual benefit corporations, covered in the following clause, or whether any comparable volunteer-immunity statute applies to religious corporation directors and officers — no such statute for religious corporations was located or verified in this research.

MUTUAL BENEFIT CORPORATION VOLUNTEER IMMUNITY IS NARROWER IN SCOPE THAN THE PUBLIC BENEFIT VERSION
A separate mutual benefit corporation statute grants a comparable immunity from monetary liability to a volunteer director or volunteer executive officer whose duties are performed in good faith, in a manner the person believes to be in the best interests of the corporation, and with the care an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances — except as the mutual benefit self-dealing statute (section 7233) or the statute governing certain loans to directors and officers (section 7236) separately provides. Unlike the public benefit corporation immunity described in the preceding clause, this statute by its own terms applies only to trade, professional, and labor organizations incorporated under the Mutual Benefit Corporation Law that operate exclusively for fraternal, educational, and other nonprofit purposes and under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c). This clause states this immunity's conditions and its scope limitation as they could apply to Jordan Lee's uncompensated service as a director of Acme, Inc., if Acme, Inc. is a mutual benefit corporation; it does not determine whether Acme, Inc. in fact falls within the trade, professional, or labor organization category the statute requires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in Section 7233 or 7236, there is no monetary liability on the part of, and no cause of action for damages shall arise against, any volunteer director or volunteer executive officer of a nonprofit corporation subject to this part based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s duties as a director or officer if the duties are performed in a manner that meets all of the following criteria: (1) The duties are performed in good faith. (2) The duties are performed in a manner such director or officer believes to be in the best interests of the corporation. (3) The duties are performed with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7231.5(a), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, volunteer director/officer immunity conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7231.5.)
  "This section shall apply only to trade, professional, and labor organizations incorporated pursuant to this part which operate exclusively for fraternal, educational, and other nonprofit purposes, and under the provisions of Section 501(c) of the United States Internal Revenue Code."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 7231.5(d), California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, scope limitation restricting this immunity to certain organizations (same section as the citation above; not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=7231.5.)
  Known gap: This is a genuine, specific scope limitation, not a boilerplate caveat: by its own subdivision (d), this statute (Corporations Code section 7231.5) does not extend to every mutual benefit corporation — a mutual benefit corporation that is not a trade, professional, or labor organization operating for the purposes and under the tax status the subdivision specifies (for example, many homeowners associations, social clubs, or membership organizations organized as mutual benefit corporations for purposes outside that description) is not shown by this statute's text to receive this immunity. This document did not locate or verify any broader volunteer-immunity statute covering other categories of mutual benefit corporations; readers should not assume this immunity applies to a mutual benefit corporation outside the described category based on this clause.

WHO MAY SUE TO ENFORCE A PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION DIRECTOR'S DUTIES
A separate statute identifies who may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for, or otherwise remedy a breach of charitable trust by a public benefit corporation: the corporation itself (or a member suing derivatively in the corporation's name, under a separately cross-referenced statute); an officer of the corporation; a director of the corporation; a person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to the charitable trust; and the Attorney General, or any person the Attorney General grants relator status. The Attorney General must be given notice of any action brought by the other listed persons and may intervene. This clause states who the statute identifies as able to bring such an action against, among others, a public benefit corporation director; it does not determine whether any specific person has standing under this statute in any specific dispute, or whether any specific conduct by Jordan Lee as a director of Acme, Inc. would constitute a breach of charitable trust.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding Section 5141, any of the following may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for or to otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust: (1) The corporation, or a member in the name of the corporation pursuant to Section 5710. (2) An officer of the corporation. (3) A director of the corporation. (4) A person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to such charitable trust. (5) The Attorney General, or any person granted relator status by the Attorney General. The Attorney General shall be given notice of any action brought by the persons specified in paragraphs (1) through (4), and may intervene."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5142(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, standing to sue for breach of charitable trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5142.)
  Known gap: This statute (Corporations Code section 5142) opens with “Notwithstanding Section 5141”; this document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 5141, so readers should not assume this clause fully states the interaction between the two sections. This document also does not verify whether a directly parallel standing statute exists for mutual benefit or religious corporations — the charitable-trust characterization this statute relies on applies to public benefit corporation assets specifically, and this document did not locate or verify a comparable statute extending the same standing categories to mutual benefit or religious corporations. No case law addressing how courts have applied this standing statute is cited anywhere in this document; a CourtListener search attempted during this research returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be retrieved.

CERTIFICATION
I certify that the description of Corporations Code sections 5231, 7231, 9241, 5239, 7231.5, and 5142 in this Information Sheet reflects the statutory text as in effect on the date below, and that this Information Sheet is a general informational reference regarding Jordan Lee's service as a director of Acme, Inc., not legal advice about, or a determination of, whether any specific act or omission by Jordan Lee satisfied the standard of care, qualified for the statutory reliance right, is protected from liability, is entitled to volunteer immunity, or could be the subject of an action to remedy a breach of duty under the statutes described above.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: _________________________
